card.blurb: A short quiz to lock in Part three and earn your XP: where data lives, references versus values, building and running, saving data, programs that talk, and keeping data safe.
hero.title: Part three checkpoint
intro.0: A short checkpoint before you move on. Answer a handful of questions on Part three - where data lives, references versus values, building and running, saving data, programs that talk, and keeping data safe - to lock it in and earn your XP.
quiz.title: Part three checkpoint
quiz.metaLabel: How software runs · Part three checkpoint
quiz.intro: Ten questions drawn from Part three - how software runs and connects. Pick the best answer for each, then submit. Score seven or more to pass and earn XP; a fresh set is drawn each time you retry.
question.1.stem: Where does a running program keep the variables and objects it is actively working with?
question.1.option.1: On disk, inside the program's file
question.1.option.3: In the operating system's own memory
question.1.why: Live data sits in RAM. The CPU holds a few values in registers at a time, but the working set lives in memory; the disk holds the program, not its live data.
question.2.stem: During a function call, where do that call's local variables live?
question.2.option.0: On the stack, in the call's frame
question.2.why: Each call gets a stack frame holding its locals; the frame - and its locals - are gone when the call returns.
question.3.stem: An object created with `new` needs to outlive the function that made it. Where does it live?
question.3.option.1: On the stack, in that function's frame
question.3.why: The heap holds objects whose lifetime is not tied to a single call; the stack frame is gone as soon as the call returns.
question.4.stem: What decides whether a variable stores its data directly, or stores a reference to it kept elsewhere?
question.4.option.0: Its type - value type versus reference type
question.4.why: The type decides: a value type holds its data in the slot; a reference type holds a reference to an object stored elsewhere.
question.5.stem: Two reference-type variables point at the same object. You change the object through one of them. The other...?
question.5.option.0: Sees the change - both reference the one object
question.5.option.1: Is unaffected - it has its own copy
question.5.why: Copying a reference copies the address, not the object - so both names reach the same object and see each other's changes.
question.6.stem: A value type is copied *by value*: `b = a` copies the data itself. You then change `a`. What is in `b`?
question.6.option.0: The original value - an independent copy
question.6.option.1: The new value - it changed too
question.6.why: A value type is copied by value, so `b` gets its own independent copy - changing `a` afterwards does not touch it.
question.7.stem: Translating your source into a runnable program - and checking its rules - happens at...?
question.7.option.0: Compile time, done by the compiler
question.7.option.1: Run time, done by the CPU
question.7.option.2: Save time, done by the editor
question.7.option.3: Startup, done by the operating system
question.7.why: The compiler translates the source and checks the rules at compile time - before the program ever runs.
question.8.stem: You break one of the language's rules. When is it caught?
question.8.option.0: At compile time - the build fails until you fix it
question.8.option.1: At run time - it crashes on that line
question.8.option.3: At save time - the editor rewrites it
question.8.why: A broken rule is a build error, caught by the compiler before the program can run - which is why many mistakes never reach users.
question.9.stem: Machine code is built for a specific target (a CPU and OS). Building, on your laptop, a program meant to run on a *different* machine is called...?
question.9.why: Cross-compiling means aiming the compiler at a target other than the machine you build on - say ARM Linux from an x64 laptop.
question.10.stem: RAM is cleared when a program stops. To keep data for next time, you...?
question.10.option.0: Write it to storage - a file on disk
question.10.option.1: Leave it in RAM and hope
question.10.why: Storage - a file on disk - survives after the program exits; RAM does not.
question.11.stem: On disk, a file is an inode plus a name. What does the inode hold?
question.11.option.0: The file's bytes and its metadata, like size and permissions
question.11.option.2: A path pointing at another file
question.11.option.3: The folder the file sits in
question.11.why: The inode is the file itself - its data plus metadata. The name is a separate directory entry that points to the inode.
question.12.stem: A directory entry that maps a name to an inode is a...?
question.12.why: A hard link is a name to inode entry; a file can have several. A soft link is different - a small file that just holds a path.
question.13.stem: One program asks another for data over a network. The message it sends and the answer it gets back are a...?
question.13.why: Programs communicate by sending a request and receiving a response - the basis of the client/server model.
question.14.stem: What is an API (application programming interface)?
question.14.option.0: The defined set of requests one program exposes for others to call
question.14.option.1: A file format stored on disk
question.14.why: An API is the interface a program offers other programs - the defined set of requests (operations) they can call, and what each returns.
question.15.stem: A single network only reaches the machines on it. What lets a program reach a server on the other side of the world?
question.15.option.0: The internet, which joins millions of networks into one
question.15.why: The internet is a network of networks - it joins millions of separate networks into one, so a request can travel far beyond the local wire.
question.16.stem: You type `example.com`, but the request needs a number like `142.250.1.14` to find the machine. What turns the name into that number?
question.16.option.0: DNS looks up the IP address behind the name
question.16.option.1: The compiler links the name at build time
question.16.option.2: The garbage collector frees the old name
question.16.option.3: The stack pushes a new frame for it
question.16.why: Every machine on the internet has an IP address. DNS is the lookup that turns a human-friendly name into that address, like a phone book.
question.17.stem: A browser and a web server both need to agree on how a request and a response are written. What set of rules do they follow?
question.17.why: HTTP is the shared set of rules the web follows - a GET request, a 200 OK response, and so on - so both sides read each other's messages the same way.
question.18.stem: Many programs must share lots of related data and change it at the same time without clashing. What do you reach for instead of a single file?
question.18.why: A database is organized storage that keeps shared data consistent under concurrent change and lets a program query for exactly the rows it needs.
question.19.stem: A password and an API key both need to stay private and must never appear in your logs. Each is an example of a...?
question.19.why: A secret is data that must stay private - a password, an API key, personal information - kept out of code and logs and never shown back.
question.20.stem: Data arrives from a web form you did not write. Before your program uses it, the safest habit is to...?
question.20.option.0: Validate it - check it is what you expect first
question.20.option.1: Trust it, since it came over HTTPS
question.20.option.2: Store it in RAM so it is faster
question.20.why: Input from outside can be wrong or hostile, so you validate it - check it is what you expect before you use it. Never trust input just because of how it arrived.
